title: Does Instructional Coaching Have a PR Problem? -pr-problem/
author: Paul Cline
summary: Paul Cline argues that instructional coaching suffers from a representation problem: the public examples used to illustrate it, entry routines, attention-getting, mini-whiteboard scripts, are overwhelmingly routine, behaviour-focused, and content-agnostic, which misrepresents the nuance of coaching done well. He traces this to practical incentives, such generic examples are easy to use in training regardless of subject, age, or phase, but argues the pattern has real costs: it fuels scepticism toward coaching by making it look simplistic, and it risks training new coaches only in superficial, performative action steps rather than the harder judgment calls coaching should develop. Cline zeroes in on the recent elevation of rehearsal as almost the defining feature of good coaching, quoting Peps Mccrea's line that coaching without rehearsal is like teaching without independent practice, and pushes back against treating rehearsal as mandatory in every session. He offers his own practice as a case study, admitting he frequently skips formal rehearsal and still sees teachers successfully implement what was discussed, while cautioning that this isn't an argument against rehearsal so much as against dogmatism about when it's needed. The piece ends by calling for richer training that shows coaches handling subject-specific, non-rehearsable problems, and for platforms that track coaching quality to stop conflating a rehearsal count with coaching effectiveness.
points: Cline argues the dominant public examples of coaching (routines, attention, behaviour scripts) are overrepresented because they're content-agnostic and easy to demonstrate, not because they're the most important part of coaching.
He directly challenges Peps Mccrea's claim that coaching without rehearsal is like teaching without independent practice, arguing the evidence for rehearsal's necessity in every case is unclear.
He discloses his own coaching practice as evidence: he sometimes skips rehearsal and still sees teachers successfully implement changes in their next lesson.
He warns that platforms measuring 'rounds of rehearsal completed' risk mistaking a proxy metric for actual coaching quality.
quotes: What’s often missing is the astonishing level of thinking that goes into the myriad decisions that teachers make on a minute-by-minute basis.
To me the issue is that the kinds of examples of action steps which relate to relatively routine, performative behaviours are over-represented in the majority of coaching illustrations.
Coaching without rehearsal is like teaching your students then not getting them to do any independent practise!
So here's my guilty confession... sometimes I don't get a teacher to do rehearsal (of a 'stand up and perform' nature) during a coaching session (though sometimes I do!).
And yet, more often than not when I drop into that teacher’s next lesson I can see them successfully implementing what we were working on.
An over-simplified representation which doesn’t appear to pay respect to the nuance and complexity of coaching could be seen to be doing the whole thing a disservice.
We need to be less dogmatic about rehearsal and acknowledge that it is a part of the coaching toolkit, and nothing more.
